title: Clear Plots and Data Visualisation
subtitle: Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: build, inspect, test, and apply the concept
description: An interactive, dashboard-focused lesson on clear plots and data visualisation, with worked code, deliberate debugging, practical transfer, and five explained application questions.

blocks.text: PAGE 1 — Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: foundations and mental model

Clear Plots and Data Visualisation is not just a syntax topic: it is a way to make the application’s intent explicit. Choose a chart type that answers a specific question, label axes and units, inspect scales, and avoid visual decoration that distorts comparisons. Check missing data before interpreting a trend. In the Code Academy dashboard, that idea matters because Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. Start by identifying the input, the rule being applied, and the result that a learner should observe. Separate what the code declares from what it actually does at runtime. A name, selector, function, condition, or query should express one clear responsibility. When reading an example, predict its behavior before running or reviewing the output. If the prediction is wrong, trace each meaningful line instead of rewriting everything at once. This habit builds the kind of reasoning that transfers to unfamiliar code, not merely a memory of one sample. The first example introduces the smallest useful version of the idea; later examples test it against variations and edge cases.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: Labels explain the measured quantity and the x-axis meaning
blocks.code:
scores <- c(85, 72, 91, 64)
plot(scores, type = "b", xlab = "Attempt", ylab = "Score", main = "Lesson scores")
blocks.output: Labels explain the measured quantity and the x-axis meaning.

blocks.text: Example 1 — line-by-line reading. Line 1 — “scores <- c(85, 72, 91, 64)”: Assigns the evaluated value to a named R object. Line 2 — “plot(scores, type = "b", xlab = "Attempt", ylab = "Score", main = "Lesson scores")”: Creates a visualization from the data and settings supplied to the plotting function. Expected behavior: Labels explain the measured quantity and the x-axis meaning. What if a line changes? Change one input or line at a time and predict the new result. Removing a required declaration, condition, selector, or query clause changes the behavior described above; never assume unchanged output without testing. This controlled experiment helps distinguish syntax, data, and logic errors.

blocks.question: A scatter plot compares study hours and exam score. Which axis labels are most informative?
options: X and Y only
No labels because the plot title exists
Labels unrelated to the variables
Study hours and Exam score, including units or scale where appropriate
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Study hours and Exam score, including units or scale where appropriate. Axis labels tell the reader what each position means.
blocks.reasoning: Axis labels tell the reader what each position means. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: A bar chart compares discrete categories using a shared scale

blocks.question: A bar chart compares counts for HTML, CSS, and Python. Which chart choice suits the data?
options: A pie chart with dozens of tiny unlabelled slices
A 3D plot that distorts bar heights
A bar plot with the course categories labelled
A line chart implying a continuous time series
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: A bar plot with the course categories labelled. Bars are a clear way to compare discrete category values.

blocks.text: PAGE 2 — Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: implementation, debugging, and edge cases

Implementation quality depends on details that are easy to miss. Choose a chart type that answers a specific question, label axes and units, inspect scales, and avoid visual decoration that distorts comparisons. Check missing data before interpreting a trend. Compare the expected result with the actual result, then ask which smallest change explains any difference. Check the data type, boundaries, execution order, and assumptions about missing or invalid input. For the Code Academy dashboard, Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. A solution that works only for one perfect input is incomplete. For instance, check empty strings, a zero count, an unavailable resource, an unknown key, or a repeated user action whenever those cases fit the feature. Keep responsibilities small so the cause of a defect can be isolated. The second and third examples show how to make the logic clearer and how to recognize a failure mode. Read the comments and output notes as a guide to reasoning, not as a substitute for inspecting every statement.

blocks.question: A histogram appears to show no low scores because missing records were dropped without disclosure. What should be done?
options: Change the bins until the desired story appears
Inspect and document missing data handling before interpreting the distribution
Assume missing scores are zero
Remove axis labels
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Inspect and document missing data handling before interpreting the distribution. Missingness can bias the observed distribution; handling should be intentional and transparent.
blocks.reasoning: Missingness can bias the observed distribution; handling should be intentional and transparent. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.question: A truncated axis exaggerates a small difference between two scores. What is the main issue?
options: The scale can mislead readers about the magnitude of the difference
A chart must always use rainbow colors
Every plot needs a 3D perspective
Axis units are unnecessary
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: The scale can mislead readers about the magnitude of the difference. A scale should support honest comparison, not visually amplify a small change.
blocks.reasoning: A scale should support honest comparison, not visually amplify a small change. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: PAGE 3 — Clear Plots and Data Visualisation: applied challenge and mastery check

Professional practice means verifying the requirement from a learner’s point of view. Choose a chart type that answers a specific question, label axes and units, inspect scales, and avoid visual decoration that distorts comparisons. Check missing data before interpreting a trend. For the Code Academy dashboard, Lesson attempts and scores can be analyzed with vectors and data frames while handling missing values explicitly. Finish by following a small test sequence: verify a normal case, a boundary case, and a failure case; confirm the page remains understandable; and check that the result matches the requirement rather than merely appearing plausible. Ask what would happen if one important line were removed, changed, or called in the wrong order. Distinguish a syntax error from a logic error and from an interface or data issue. The final sample brings the concept into a compact applied task, and the questions ask for decisions rather than isolated definitions. A strong answer should be supported by a reason and by a test that could prove or disprove the assumption.

Applied challenge: implement a small Code Academy feature that uses clear plots and data visualisation. Define the expected behavior in one sentence, identify the input and output, and choose the simplest code pattern above that fits. Test a normal case and an edge case. Then make one controlled change: remove a condition, alter a value, or change an input shape. Record what breaks and explain why. This is the “do and let me do” part of the lesson: the concept becomes memorable when the learner predicts a result, observes it, and explains the difference.

blocks.question: A plot is technically correct but its meaning is unclear. What is the best next step?
options: Add decorative shadows
Remove the legend even if colors are ambiguous
Use smaller text for all labels
Add a purposeful title, axis labels, units, and appropriate scale
blocks.explanation: Correct answer: Add a purposeful title, axis labels, units, and appropriate scale. Readable labeling makes the data relationship interpretable.
blocks.reasoning: Readable labeling makes the data relationship interpretable. Apply the rule to a real dashboard scenario, then test both ordinary and boundary inputs.

blocks.text: Lesson recap: Choose a chart type that answers a specific question, label axes and units, inspect scales, and avoid visual decoration that distorts comparisons. Check missing data before interpreting a trend. Keep the underlying rule in mind when moving to more complex dashboard features. Syntax is the visible surface; reliable reasoning, validation, and testing are the transferable skill.
